beginner.headline: Tech Share Prices Fall After US Elections
beginner.brief: Share prices for big tech companies fell in the US and Asia after the US elections. People worried that work on artificial intelligence, or AI, might slow down. Some Democrats wanted to slow down the building of new data centres. These centres help run AI. People also wondered if all the spending on AI would be worth it. In Japan, shares in the chip maker Kioxia fell by more than 12%. Buying and selling shares on the Seoul market stopped for a short time after share prices fell fast.

intermediate.headline: Tech Stocks Slide as US Midterms Raise AI Concerns
intermediate.brief: Tech stocks in the US and Asia dropped sharply after the US midterms raised fears that artificial intelligence (AI) development could slow. Democrats across the US campaigned to limit the growth of AI and data centres, the facilities that help power the technology. Democrats won control of both houses of Congress, the Senate and the House of Representatives. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for governor, had promised to put new data centre construction on hold. The Nasdaq Composite, an index that tracks a group of stocks, closed more than 5.5% lower. In Japan, the Nikkei 225 was down 6% in early trading as shares in chip companies Kioxia and Tokyo Electron lost value. In Seoul, the sell-off pushed the Kospi index down more than 8.5%, leading to a brief pause in trading to limit panic selling. Investors were already questioning whether the large sums going into AI would pay off. Investment strategist Charu Chanana said closer checks on data centre plans could delay projects and raise costs. Chanana pointed to the effects of data centres on the environment and on electricity bills as issues that could face closer review. OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman said more work was needed to win support from local communities.

advanced.headline: Tech Stocks Slide as US Midterms Stir AI Fears
advanced.brief: Major technology stocks in the United States and Asia plunged after the US midterm elections raised concerns that AI development could slow. The technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended the trading day more than 5.5% below its previous close, according to Dow Jones data. The drop put the Nasdaq Composite in correction territory, meaning it was at least 10% below its recent high. In South Korea, the Kospi dropped more than 8.5%, triggering a circuit breaker that temporarily halted trading in an effort to curb panic selling. Dozens of ballot measures across the United States sought to restrict the development of data centres, the facilities that provide computing power for AI. In Texas, Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa pledged a moratorium on new data centre construction. Investors weighed the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction alongside concerns that AI infrastructure might yield lower returns than they had counted on. Charu Chanana said greater scrutiny of data centre approvals and of the projects’ effects on the environment and electricity bills could delay projects and drive up costs across the industry. Although both parties want the United States to lead in AI, support for the technology leaves open the question of how quickly and at what cost its infrastructure should expand, Chanana said. Some technology leaders said the backlash against data centres in the midterms had taken them by surprise. OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said more work was needed to secure the backing of local communities.
